actions.name: Review home BP log
actions.result: Home BP log (30 days): readings range 148-172/88-98, average 158/92 mmHg; heart rate 72-80 bpm; measured morning and evening per patient report.

actions.name: Review current medication list in chart
actions.result: Losartan 100 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, insulin glargine 24 units nightly, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. No NSAID or supplement listed.

actions.name: Review most recent comprehensive metabolic panel
actions.result: Sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L (H), chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (L), BUN 48 mg/dL (H), creatinine 2.9 mg/dL (H), eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m2 (L), glucose 162 mg/dL (H), calcium 8.9 mg/dL, phosphate 5.2 mg/dL (H).

actions.name: Review urine albumin-creatinine ratio trend
actions.result: Urine ACR 1,850 mg/g (H), up from 1,210 mg/g 6 months ago and 740 mg/g 12 months ago.

actions.name: Review complete blood count
actions.result: Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL (L), hematocrit 30.5% (L), MCV 88 fL, platelets 240 x10^3/uL, WBC 6.8 x10^3/uL.

actions.name: Review lipid panel
actions.result: Total cholesterol 165 mg/dL, LDL 88 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL (L), triglycerides 195 mg/dL (H).

actions.name: Review renal ultrasound report
actions.result: Kidneys measure 9.2 cm (right) and 9.0 cm (left) with increased cortical echogenicity and mild cortical thinning bilaterally; no hydronephrosis, no masses or stones.

actions.name: Guided camera inspection of arms for vascular access sites
actions.result: Patient shows both forearms on camera; veins appear small but visible on inspection, no scars or prior access, skin intact, no edema at wrist.

actions.name: Guided self-exam for peripheral edema
actions.result: Patient presses on own shins on camera; mild pitting edema noted at both ankles (1+), resolves slowly.

actions.name: Camera inspection of skin and general appearance
actions.result: Alert, conversational, no acute distress, no pallor of conjunctivae visible, no asterixis on arm extension test, no uremic fetor reported by patient.

actions.name: Review home glucose log
actions.result: Home fingerstick glucose log: fasting values 140-190 mg/dL, occasional readings over 220 mg/dL after meals, no documented hypoglycemia.

actions.name: Calculate CKD stage and risk category
actions.result: CKD stage G4A3 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m2, albuminuria category A3). Rapid progression per KDIGO criteria (eGFR decline of ~8 mL/min/1.73m2/year, exceeding the >5 mL/min/1.73m2/year threshold). Kidney Failure Risk Equation (4-variable, using age 58, male sex, eGFR 22, ACR 1,850 mg/g) calculated this visit: estimated 2-year risk of kidney failure approximately 40-45% and 5-year risk approximately 70-75%, confirming very high risk and supporting prompt referral for transplant evaluation and vascular access/modality planning.

actions.name: Review home urine dipstick (if performed)
actions.result: Patient does not have a urine dipstick at home; test not performed this visit.

actions.name: Review prior nephrology note for education discussed
actions.result: Prior note documents CKD stage 3b-4 diagnosis and medication reconciliation; no documentation of transplant, dialysis modality, or vascular access planning discussion to date.

actions.name: Screen readiness for kidney replacement therapy education
actions.result: Patient becomes visibly guarded and anxious when kidney replacement therapy is mentioned, brief pause and tightened expression; no prior exposure to transplant or home dialysis options documented. Underlying beliefs and concerns not yet verbalized; direct, empathetic questioning needed to explore further.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Rapidly progressing CKD stage G4A3 (likely diabetic + hypertensive nephropathy) with hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism risk, complicated by NSAID and herbal nephrotoxin exposure, poorly controlled BP and glucose, and unaddressed fear-driven avoidance of kidney replacement therapy planning.
differential: Diabetic nephropathy with superimposed hypertensive nephrosclerosis
NSAID-induced chronic tubulointerstitial injury accelerating decline
Herbal/'kidney cleanse' supplement nephrotoxicity (unregulated, unknown contents, possible aristolochic acid or other nephrotoxins)
Volume-mediated hyperkalemia from ACE/ARB therapy combined with reduced GFR and possible dietary potassium
Underlying glomerular disease requiring further workup if proteinuria disproportionate to diabetes duration/control
keyFindings: eGFR declined from 34 to 22 mL/min/1.73m2 over 18 months - rapid progression
Urine ACR rising from 740 to 1,210 to 1,850 mg/g over 12 months
Potassium 5.4 mmol/L and bicarbonate 18 mmol/L indicating hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis
Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL consistent with CKD-related anemia
Phosphate 5.2 mg/dL elevated, concerning for early mineral bone disease
Home BP averaging 158/92, above CKD target despite two antihypertensives
Daily naproxen use and unregulated herbal 'kidney cleanse' supplement, both nephrotoxic and unlisted in chart
A1c 8.4% reflecting suboptimal glycemic control contributing to progression
No prior discussion of transplant, home dialysis, or vascular access planning despite advanced CKD
Strong, fear-based refusal of dialysis rooted in family experience, not yet explored or addressed
plan: Counsel patient to stop naproxen immediately; coordinate with primary care for non-nephrotoxic pain management alternative for prolonged standing (e.g., acetaminophen, topical agents, PT referral)
Advise discontinuation of unregulated 'kidney cleanse' herbal supplement; explain unknown contents can accelerate kidney damage

Address hyperkalemia: review diet, consider dose adjustment of ACE/ARB only after addressing reversible contributors, recheck potassium in short interval, consider potassium binder if needed within scope
Address metabolic acidosis: consider initiating sodium bicarbonate supplementation per CKD guidelines
Optimize blood pressure: review home BP log, consider adjusting antihypertensive regimen with PCP/cardiology coordination, reinforce home monitoring technique
Coordinate with endocrinology/PCP on glycemic optimization given A1c 8.4%
Initiate workup/monitoring for CKD-related anemia and mineral bone disease (iron studies, PTH, vitamin D as per CKD-MBD protocol)

Begin structured, non-coercive kidney replacement therapy education: explore the patient's fear and his uncle's dialysis experience, introduce options including home dialysis modalities, transplant evaluation referral, and conservative care, without forcing a decision today
Refer for transplant evaluation given eligibility and advanced CKD trajectory
Discuss early vascular access planning conceptually without committing patient to a modality, emphasizing that planning preserves future options
Schedule close follow-up (4-6 weeks) to reassess labs, BP control, and continue modality education
Refer to renal dietitian for potassium/phosphate/protein counseling
redFlags: Potassium 5.4 mmol/L with concurrent ARB use - monitor for progression to dangerous hyperkalemia
Rapid eGFR decline (34 to 22 over 18 months) suggesting accelerated progression needing urgent intervention
Unregulated herbal supplement use with nephrotoxic potential
Complete absence of kidney replacement therapy and transplant education despite advanced CKD - access/transplant planning window closing
Daily NSAID use in setting of CKD stage 4
educationPoints: CKD progression can be accelerated by seemingly minor behaviors like daily OTC NSAID use and unregulated supplements, which patients may not think to mention or list as 'medications'
Fear of dialysis based on a family member's negative experience is common and deserves exploration, not dismissal; education should be modality-inclusive and non-coercive
Transplant evaluation and home dialysis options should be introduced early (CKD G4) rather than waiting until G5, to preserve all options including preemptive transplant and timely access planning
Discrepancies between the medication list and patient-reported self-treatment (NSAIDs, supplements) are common and require explicit, non-judgmental questioning
Multidisciplinary coordination (PCP, endocrinology, dietitian) is essential in managing the multiple drivers of CKD progression in this patient

cells: less than 5.7 (goal individualized, typically less than 7-7.5 in CKD)

artifacts.title: Renal Ultrasound Report
artifacts.author: Detroit Medical Imaging Center
artifacts.body:
RENAL ULTRASOUND WITHOUT DOPPLER

Indication: Chronic kidney disease, evaluate for structural abnormality.

Findings: Right kidney measures 9.2 cm in length, left kidney measures 9.0 cm in length. Bilateral increased cortical echogenicity with mild cortical thinning, consistent with chronic medical renal disease. No hydronephrosis. No renal calculi. No solid or cystic renal masses identified. Bladder appears unremarkable on limited views.

Impression: Findings consistent with chronic parenchymal kidney disease. No obstructive uropathy or mass lesion.

artifacts.author: Dr. A. Reyes, Nephrology
artifacts.body:
CC: CKD follow-up.

Assessment: 58-year-old male with CKD stage 3b-4 secondary to diabetes and hypertension, eGFR 26 at last check. Reviewed medications: losartan, amlodipine, insulin glargine, atorvastatin - no changes made. Discussed importance of blood pressure control and glycemic control. Patient reports doing well overall. Plan: continue current regimen, recheck labs in 6 months, renal ultrasound ordered.

Note: No documentation this visit of discussion regarding kidney replacement therapy options, transplant referral, or vascular access planning.

facts.chart: Patient presents for CKD follow-up to review kidney function labs and blood pressure.
facts.says: My doctor's office said my kidney numbers came back worse and I need to talk to you about it.

facts.chart: Reports feeling generally well, denies significant fatigue, nausea, or appetite change.
facts.says: Honestly I feel pretty normal. Tired sometimes but I figured that's just from being on my feet all day cutting hair.

facts.chart: Reports mild ankle swelling by end of workday, improves overnight.
facts.says: My ankles puff up a little by the end of the day standing in the shop, but they look normal by morning.

facts.chart: Denies changes in urine color, foam, or frequency; denies gross hematuria.

facts.chart: Takes naproxen 220 mg over-the-counter, typically 2 tablets most days, for back and leg pain from standing at work; not listed on medication reconciliation.
facts.says: I take some naproxen most days, maybe twice a day, because my back and legs kill me from standing all day cutting hair. I didn't think to mention it since you can just buy it at the store.

facts.chart: Uses an herbal 'kidney cleanse' supplement recommended by a customer, taken daily for approximately 2 months; ingredients unknown, not listed on medication reconciliation.
facts.says: A customer of mine swears by this kidney cleanse tea and capsules, says it flushed his kidneys right out. I've been taking it about two months now hoping it'd help.

facts.chart: Reports taking losartan, amlodipine, insulin glargine, and atorvastatin as prescribed, occasionally misses evening insulin dose when working late.
facts.says: I take my pills pretty much every day. Sometimes I forget my nighttime insulin shot if I'm closing up the shop late.

facts.chart: Checks home blood pressure most mornings and some evenings using a pharmacy-purchased cuff; readings consistently elevated.
facts.says: I check it most mornings on my own cuff. It's always running high, like 150s, 160s, sometimes higher.

facts.chart: Diet includes frequent takeout and canned foods due to long work hours; limited home cooking.
facts.says: Honestly between the shop and everything I eat a lot of takeout, some canned soups and stuff, don't always have time to cook.

facts.chart: Reports home fingerstick glucose readings often in 140-190 mg/dL range, sometimes higher after meals.
facts.says: My sugars run kind of high, like 140s to 190s most mornings, sometimes it spikes after I eat something I shouldn't.

facts.chart: Patient's uncle underwent hemodialysis and died while on dialysis; patient attributes death directly to the dialysis treatment itself.
facts.says: My uncle went on that machine and he died on it. I watched him go downhill. I made up my mind a long time ago, I'm never doing that.

facts.chart: Describes feeling rushed and unheard in prior clinic visits; expresses some mistrust of the healthcare system.
facts.says: Last time I went in, doc barely looked at me, just typed on the computer and sent me out. I've learned to just go with what I already know.

facts.chart: States clear preference to avoid dialysis under any circumstances; has not considered or heard about transplant or home dialysis options.
facts.says: I don't care what the numbers say, I'm not doing dialysis. Nobody's ever mentioned any other options to me anyway.

facts.chart: Owns and operates a barbershop, works 6 days a week, 10-12 hour days, standing most of the time.
facts.says: I own my shop, been cutting hair over 30 years. I'm there six days a week, long hours, mostly on my feet.

facts.chart: Has health insurance through a small business plan but worries about cost of additional specialist visits and tests.
facts.says: I've got insurance through my business plan but it's not the greatest, I worry about piling up more appointments and bills.

facts.chart: Diagnosed with type 2 diabetes approximately 14 years ago.
facts.says: I've had the sugar diabetes for about 14 years now.

facts.chart: Diagnosed with hypertension approximately 16 years ago.
facts.says: High blood pressure's been with me even longer, maybe 16 years.

facts.chart: Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, orthopnea, or palpitations.
facts.says: No chest pain or trouble breathing, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Reports chronic low back and leg pain attributed to standing, longstanding, unchanged recently; distractor for an unrelated musculoskeletal complaint rather than CKD-MBD at this point.
facts.says: My back and legs have ached for years from this job, nothing new there.

facts.chart: Reports occasional mild blurry vision, attributes to needing new reading glasses; no recent diabetic eye exam.
facts.says: My eyes get a little blurry sometimes, probably just need new reading glasses, haven't been to the eye doctor in a while.

facts.chart: Drinks beer socially, approximately 2-3 beers on weekends, denies daily drinking.
facts.says: I'll have a couple beers on the weekend with friends, nothing during the week though.

facts.chart: Former smoker, quit approximately 10 years ago, previously smoked about 1 pack per day for 15 years.
facts.says: I used to smoke, quit about 10 years back. Before that it was close to a pack a day for 15 years.

facts.chart: Mother had hypertension; father had type 2 diabetes; uncle had end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis.
facts.says: My mom had high blood pressure, my dad had the sugar too, and then there's my uncle with his kidneys.

facts.chart: Reports no limitation in daily activities or exercise tolerance beyond baseline fatigue from long work hours.
facts.says: I can still do everything I need to do at the shop, no real limits on what I can do.

facts.chart: Has moderate understanding that kidneys are 'not working as well' but unclear on stage, prognosis, or treatment pathway differences.
facts.says: I know my kidneys aren't doing so hot, but nobody's really broken down for me what happens next or what my choices even are.

facts.chart: Has not disclosed the herbal supplement or naproxen use to primary care physician either.
facts.says: I never brought up the cleanse or the naproxen to my regular doctor, didn't think it mattered since they're not prescription.

facts.chart: Denies erectile dysfunction or other sexual health concerns at this time.
facts.says: No issues in that department, no complaints there.

facts.chart: Describes drawing strength from his church community and faith when coping with health stress.
facts.says: My church family keeps me grounded through all this, I lean on my faith a lot.

facts.chart: Denies significant unintentional weight loss or anorexia; reports stable appetite.
facts.says: My appetite's fine, eating about the same as always, haven't lost weight or anything.

facts.chart: Expresses strong desire to continue working and is worried any kidney treatment would force him to close his shop.
facts.says: This shop is everything to me, I built it from nothing. I'm scared whatever you tell me to do is gonna mean I can't work anymore.

facts.chart: Reports sometimes taking amlodipine late or skipping if he forgets while busy at the shop, roughly once a week.
facts.says: Sometimes I forget the amlodipine if it's a crazy day at the shop, maybe once a week I miss it.

facts.chart: Recalls previous nephrology visit focused only on labs and medication refills without discussion of long-term kidney treatment options.
facts.says: Last time with the kidney doctor, we just went over the numbers and refilled my pills, didn't really talk about down the road.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he takes his prescribed medications, including amlodipine, pretty much every day and checks that his blood pressure control is reasonable from his perspective.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Home blood pressure log shows consistently elevated readings (148-172/88-98) over 30 days despite being on losartan and amlodipine, suggesting either inadequate regimen, non-adherence, or both.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often does not match objective BP control; the fellow should reconcile the home log with the medication list and explore adherence gaps (confirmed later as occasional missed amlodipine doses) rather than assuming the regimen alone is failing.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports feeling generally well with no significant symptoms, framing his fatigue as purely due to his work schedule.
mismatches.recordEvidence: eGFR trend chart shows a steep, consistent decline from 34 to 22 mL/min/1.73m2 over 18 months, a trajectory inconsistent with a stable, asymptomatic course and warranting urgent evaluation for reversible contributors.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients with CKD are frequently asymptomatic even with rapidly progressive disease; clinicians must rely on objective trends rather than symptom absence to judge urgency, and should actively search for reversible causes such as NSAID or nephrotoxin exposure.

objectives.text: Identify and reconcile medication discrepancies, including unlisted over-the-counter NSAID use and herbal supplement use, as contributors to accelerated CKD progression.
Interpret trends in eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio to correctly stage CKD and recognize the rapid progression warranting urgent action.
Recognize and address complications of advanced CKD including hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism risk.

Through direct, empathetic questioning, elicit and respectfully explore the patient's fear-based refusal of dialysis rooted in family experience, and recognize the gap in prior kidney replacement therapy education.
Identify a discrepancy between patient-reported medication adherence/wellness and objective home blood pressure and lab trends, and respond without judgment.

Formulate an appropriate nephrology-scope management plan including stopping nephrotoxic exposures, correcting electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities, coordinating multidisciplinary care, and initiating non-coercive transplant and modality education with appropriate referrals.

patient.name: Curtis Washington
patient.appearance: A broad-shouldered man with greying short hair and a neatly trimmed beard, wearing a collared barbershop polo shirt. He appears on camera seated in a small back office of his shop, shelves with hair products visible behind him, lighting slightly dim. His posture is upright and he gestures animatedly when talking, though his expression tightens when the topic of dialysis comes up.

persona.personality: Proud, sociable, hardworking, protective of his independence, carries guarded skepticism toward the medical system from past experiences.
persona.communicationStyle: Talks in a warm, conversational, storytelling way; uses plain everyday language; can become clipped and defensive when he feels judged or rushed.
persona.emotionalState: Generally upbeat and friendly at the start, but becomes anxious and guarded when dialysis or 'the machine' comes up, and slightly embarrassed when supplement or NSAID use is uncovered.
persona.background: Curtis has owned his barbershop in Detroit for over 30 years, built it up from a single chair to a full shop with three other barbers. He's active in his church and known in the neighborhood for cutting hair for three generations of some families. He raised two kids who are now grown, and he takes pride in being the guy people come to for advice as much as a haircut.
speechExamples: I've been cutting hair in this neighborhood since before some of my customers were born.
Doc, I hear you, but I watched my uncle go through that machine and I made my peace with not doing that to myself.
I didn't think the store-bought stuff counted as a real medicine, you know?
My shop is my life, I can't be hooked up to some machine three days a week and still run this place.
Appreciate you taking the time, last place I went felt like they just wanted me out the door.
concerns: Fear that any kidney treatment will mean dialysis and losing his ability to work
Worry that bringing up the herbal supplement or NSAID use will get him judged or lectured
General mistrust of being rushed through visits without being heard
Confusion about what options exist besides dialysis
Concern about cost and time burden of additional specialist appointments

scenario.studentBrief: You are a nephrology fellow conducting a telehealth follow-up visit with Curtis Washington, a 58-year-old man with CKD from diabetes and hypertension. Review his recent labs, blood pressure trends, and medications, and address next steps in his care.
scenario.chiefComplaint: CKD follow-up after labs show worsening kidney function
scenario.openingLine: Hey doc, thanks for fitting me in between clients. My regular doctor's office said my kidney numbers came back worse and that you'd want to talk to me about what's next.
tasks: Review and interpret the trend in eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio
Reconcile the medication list with what the patient is actually taking, including any over-the-counter drugs or supplements
Identify and address modifiable contributors to CKD progression
Explore the patient's understanding and concerns about kidney disease progression
Develop and clearly communicate a follow-up plan including appropriate referrals

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at a small back office inside his barbershop in Detroit, Michigan during a break between clients
profile.summary: A 58-year-old Detroit barber with diabetic and hypertensive CKD shows rapid eGFR decline (34 to 22 mL/min/1.73m2 over 18 months) with worsening albuminuria, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and anemia, compounded by undisclosed daily NSAID and herbal supplement use. The case centers on uncovering hidden nephrotoxic exposures, reconciling patient-reported adherence against objective BP/lab trends, and respectfully opening a long-overdue conversation about kidney replacement therapy options after the patient's fear-driven refusal of dialysis based on a family member's death.
profile.title: Rapidly Progressive CKD and Overdue Kidney Replacement Therapy Counseling in a 58-Year-Old Barber
